items.ask: List the assumptions of Euler-Bernoulli beam theory.
items.answer: 1) Plane sections stay plane. 2) Sections stay perpendicular to the deformed axis (transverse shear strain zero). 3) Small strains and small slopes. 4) Linear elastic, homogeneous material. 5) Slender beam, L ≫ h. 6) Transverse normal stresses negligible.
items.cue: Picture a deck of cards drawn on the side of a beam: each card line stays straight and square to the bent axis.

items.ask: Where is the neutral axis of a homogeneous beam in pure bending, and which equation puts it there?
items.answer: Through the centroid of the cross section. Pure bending has zero net axial force, ∫σ dA = (E/ρ)∫y dA = 0, so the first moment of area about the neutral axis is zero.
items.cue: Zero axial force means tension and compression areas balance like a seesaw about the centroid.

items.ask: State the boundary conditions for a clamped, a pinned and a free end of an Euler-Bernoulli beam.
items.answer: Clamped: w = 0, w′ = 0. Pinned (simple support): w = 0, M = EIw″ = 0. Free: M = EIw″ = 0, V = (EIw″)′ = 0. Two conditions at every end.
items.cue: Clamped grips the geometry, free releases the forces, pinned takes one of each.

items.ask: With q positive downward, sagging moment positive and shear positive when it turns the element clockwise, state the load, shear and moment relations.
items.answer: dV/dx = −q and dM/dx = V, so d²M/dx² = −q. The moment is extreme where the shear is zero.
items.cue: Moment slope equals shear: the peak of the moment diagram sits where the shear diagram crosses zero.

items.ask: Give the transverse shear stress in a beam and its peak value for a rectangular section.
items.answer: τ = VQ/(It), with Q the first moment of the area beyond the cut. For a rectangle the distribution is parabolic, zero at the top and bottom, peak at the neutral axis: τ_max = 3V/(2A).
items.cue: Bending stress peaks at the skin, shear stress peaks at the middle: the two share the job across the depth.

items.ask: Define principal axes of a cross section and name one quick way to identify one.
items.answer: Centroidal axes about which the product of inertia I_xy = 0, so bending about each one decouples. Any axis of symmetry is a principal axis, and the axis perpendicular to it is the other.
items.cue: A mirror line of the section always lies along a principal axis: the products from each side cancel.

items.ask: Define the section modulus and give the peak bending stress in terms of it.
items.answer: S = I/c, with c the distance from the neutral axis to the extreme fiber. σ_max = M/S. For a rectangle S = bh²/6.
items.cue: Rectangle: bh³/12 divided by h/2 gives bh²/6. Depth squared rewards deep beams.

items.ask: Define the shear center.
items.answer: The point in the cross section through which a transverse load causes bending with zero twist. The resultant of the shear flow from bending always acts through it. It lies on every axis of symmetry.
items.cue: Push a channel through its shear center and it bends straight down, keeping its face square to you.

items.ask: List the steps to locate the shear center of a thin-walled open section.
items.answer: 1) Find the centroid and I. 2) Apply shear V at an unknown point e. 3) Build q(s) = (V/I)∫y t ds starting at a free edge where q = 0. 4) Integrate q into wall resultants. 5) Moments about a convenient point equal V e. 6) Solve for e.
items.cue: Free edge first, flow builds, walls become forces, moments balance V e.

items.ask: Give the shear center offset of a channel with uniform thickness, flange width b and web height h.
items.answer: e = 3b²/(h + 6b), measured from the web centerline, on the side opposite the flanges (outside the section). It follows from e = b²h²t/(4I).
items.cue: The flange shear forces form a couple about the web; V acts behind the web, away from the flanges, to cancel it.

items.ask: Where is the shear center of a section made of thin straight walls meeting at a single point, such as an angle or a T?
items.answer: At the intersection of the wall centerlines. Every wall shear flow resultant passes through that point, so their moment about it is zero.
items.cue: All forces aim through one corner, so that corner is the twist-free load point.

items.ask: State the assumptions behind the Bredt-Batho formula for a single closed cell.
items.answer: Thin wall, shear stress uniform through the thickness and tangent to the wall, pure torsion with zero axial stress (free warping), so axial equilibrium makes the shear flow q constant around the cell; cross section shape preserved.
items.cue: Thin wall, uniform τ, free warping: then q is constant, like a current flowing around a single loop.

items.ask: How do you solve an n-cell closed section in pure torsion?
items.answer: Unknowns: one shear flow per cell, q₁ to qₙ. Equations: torque T = Σ 2Aᵢqᵢ, plus n − 1 compatibility equations setting the twist rate θ′ = (1/(2AᵢG))∮q ds/t equal in every cell. Shared walls carry the difference of adjacent flows.
items.cue: One torque equation plus equal twist in every cell: the cells are welded together, so they rotate as one.

items.ask: For a thin circular tube of radius R and thickness t, compare torsion constants of the closed tube and the same tube slit lengthwise.
items.answer: Closed: J = 2πR³t. Slit (open): J = 2πRt³/3. Ratio closed/open = 3(R/t)², about 30,000 for R/t = 100.
items.cue: Closed gets R², open gets t²: a slit drinking straw twists like paper.

items.ask: State the membrane analogy for torsion.
items.answer: A membrane stretched over the section outline and inflated: deflection corresponds to the stress function ψ, the slope magnitude to the shear stress, contour lines give the stress direction (tangent), and twice the enclosed volume gives the torque T.
items.cue: Soap bubble on the section: steepest slope, highest stress; bigger bubble volume, bigger torque.

items.ask: In a solid noncircular section under torsion, where is the shear stress largest and where is it zero?
items.answer: Largest on the boundary at the point closest to the centroid (mid-side of the long side of a rectangle, mid-sides of a triangle). Zero at convex (outward) corners.
items.cue: Membrane is steepest where the wall is nearest the center and flat in the corners.

items.ask: State Castigliano's first and second theorems.
items.answer: First: Pᵢ = ∂U/∂δᵢ, with strain energy U written in terms of displacements. Second: δᵢ = ∂U*/∂Pᵢ, with complementary energy U* written in terms of loads; U* = U for linear elastic structures.
items.cue: First: displacement in, force out. Second: force in, displacement out. Each derivative swaps to the conjugate.

items.ask: List the steps of the unit load method for one deflection.
items.answer: 1) Real loads: find M(x) (and N, T). 2) Remove them; apply a unit load at the point, along the wanted displacement: find m(x). 3) δ = ∫Mm/(EI) dx plus axial and torsion terms. 4) A positive δ acts in the direction of the unit load.
items.cue: Point the unit load where you want to look; the answer comes out in that direction.

items.ask: State the principles of virtual displacements and virtual forces, and what each one yields.
items.answer: Virtual displacements: δW_int = δW_ext for every kinematically admissible virtual displacement; this is equivalent to equilibrium. Virtual forces: complementary virtual work balances for every statically admissible virtual force system; this is equivalent to compatibility.
items.cue: Virtual displacement tests forces, giving equilibrium. Virtual force tests geometry, giving compatibility. Each probes the opposite.

items.ask: Contrast the total potential energy (TPE) and total complementary potential energy (TCPE) principles.
items.answer: TPE: Π = U − W, varied over kinematically admissible displacements; stationarity gives equilibrium. TCPE: Π* = U* − Σ R ū, varied over statically admissible forces; stationarity gives compatibility. Both are minima at the stable solution.
items.cue: TPE picks displacements and enforces forces; TCPE picks forces and enforces fit. Least work is TCPE.

items.ask: Distinguish essential and natural boundary conditions in a Ritz analysis.
items.answer: Essential (kinematic): prescribed displacements and slopes; the trial functions must satisfy them. Natural (force): prescribed moment, shear and spring reactions; they emerge from δΠ = 0. A spring support adds ½ku² to Π and is a natural condition.
items.cue: Essential is built into the shape; natural arrives on its own from minimizing energy.

items.ask: List the steps of a Rayleigh-Ritz analysis of a beam.
items.answer: 1) Choose w = Σaᵢφᵢ satisfying the essential BCs. 2) Write Π = ∫½EIw″² dx + spring energies − ∫qw dx − ΣPw. 3) Substitute and integrate. 4) Set ∂Π/∂aᵢ = 0. 5) Solve Ka = f. 6) Recover w, M and check.
items.cue: Shape, energy, integrate, differentiate, solve. Loads enter Π with a minus sign because they lose potential as they move.

items.ask: Which way do Ritz results err, and what happens as you add trial terms?
items.answer: The Ritz model is stiffer than the true structure: Π_Ritz ≥ Π_exact, the deflection under a single point load is a lower bound, and the buckling load is an upper bound. Adding terms lowers Π monotonically toward the exact value.
items.cue: A restricted shape is a constraint, and constraints stiffen: smaller deflection, higher buckling load.

items.ask: Define strain energy density and complementary energy density, and state when they are equal.
items.answer: U₀ = ∫₀^ε σ dε (area under the σ-ε curve). U₀* = ∫₀^σ ε dσ (area to the left of it). Equal for linear elastic material, where each is ½σε.
items.cue: Two triangles splitting the rectangle σε: below the curve is U, beside it is U*.

items.ask: State Clapeyron's theorem.
items.answer: For a linear elastic structure loaded gradually from zero, U = ½ΣPᵢδᵢ, with δᵢ the displacement at load Pᵢ along its direction.
items.cue: Spring with force growing linearly from zero: area of the triangle is half of force times stretch.

items.ask: Distinguish a bifurcation point from a limit point.
items.answer: Bifurcation: two equilibrium paths intersect; the primary path continues and a secondary (buckled) path branches off. Limit point: a single path reaches a load maximum, dP/dq = 0; under load control the structure snaps through to a distant configuration.
items.cue: Bifurcation is a fork in the road; a limit point is the summit of a single hill road.

items.ask: Define a stable symmetric bifurcation and give an example.
items.answer: The post-buckling path is symmetric in ±ξ and rises: P/P_c ≈ 1 + bξ², b > 0. Imperfect structures deform smoothly and keep carrying load above P_c. Examples: rigid bar with a base rotational spring (P/P_cr = θ/sin θ), Euler column, flat plate.
items.cue: Smiling parabola: b positive, the load path curves up both ways.

items.ask: Define an unstable symmetric bifurcation and give an example.
items.answer: The post-buckling path is symmetric in ±ξ and falls: P/P_c ≈ 1 + bξ², b < 0. The imperfect structure reaches a limit load below P_c, reduced by the two-thirds law. Example: pinned rigid bar with a horizontal spring at the top, P = kL cos θ.
items.cue: Frowning parabola: b negative, the load path droops both ways.

items.ask: Define an asymmetric bifurcation and give an example.
items.answer: The post-buckling path crosses P_c with a finite slope: P/P_c ≈ 1 + aξ, a ≠ 0. It rises (stable) on one side and falls (unstable) on the other. Imperfections toward the falling side give a limit load reduced by the one-half power law. Example: L-shaped (Roorda) frame.
items.cue: A tilted line through the fork: one side climbs, the other slides down.

items.ask: State the two-thirds power law.
items.answer: For an unstable symmetric bifurcation, the limit load P_s of the imperfect structure satisfies 1 − P_s/P_c ∝ ε^(2/3), with ε the imperfection amplitude. The asymmetric case follows the one-half power: 1 − P_s/P_c ∝ ε^(1/2).
items.cue: Symmetric has two equal sides: two-thirds. Asymmetric has one bad side: one-half, the square root.

items.ask: When does the static method give the critical load, and when is the kinetic method required?
items.answer: Static (adjacent equilibrium or energy) method: conservative loads, where it matches the kinetic result. Kinetic method: nonconservative loads such as follower loads; study small vibrations about equilibrium. Instability is divergence (a frequency reaches zero) or flutter (two frequencies coalesce). Beck's column: P_cr ≈ 20.05EI/L².
items.cue: A follower force has a moving target, so check if it shakes apart: watch the frequencies.

items.ask: Define a conservative load and a follower load.
items.answer: Conservative: the work done depends only on the end configuration, so the load has a potential; a dead load keeps a fixed direction and magnitude. Follower load: its direction turns with the deforming structure (a thrust along a bent tip), making it path dependent and nonconservative.
items.cue: Dead weight always points down; a rocket on a bending tip pushes along the tip.

items.ask: Name the methods of elastic stability analysis.
items.answer: 1) Equilibrium (adjacent equilibrium, Euler) method. 2) Energy method: δΠ = 0 and the sign of δ²Π. 3) Kinetic (dynamic) method: small vibrations about equilibrium. 4) Imperfection method: follow the load-deflection path of a slightly imperfect structure.
items.cue: Four ways to ask if the ball stays in the bowl: balance it, weigh energy, shake it, or tilt it slightly.

items.ask: State the seven-rung ladder for a rigid-bar spring stability problem.
items.answer: 1) Write Π = U − PΔ with every term. 2) Equilibrium: dΠ/dθ = 0. 3) Linearize about θ = 0. 4) Solve for P_cr. 5) Stability of the trivial path from d²Π/dθ². 6) Post-buckling: expand to θ⁴. 7) Imperfection sensitivity.
items.cue: Energy, equilibrium, linearize, critical, check, post-buckle, imperfect: E-E-L-C-C-P-I.

items.ask: For the rigid-bar ladder, give the small-angle expansions and the role of each order in Π.
items.answer: cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2 + θ⁴/24, sin θ ≈ θ − θ³/6. Keep every term in Π to θ⁴. The θ² terms locate P_cr; the θ⁴ terms decide the post-buckling curvature (stable or unstable symmetric); a θ³ term signals an asymmetric bifurcation.
items.cue: Quadratic finds the cliff edge; quartic tells which way the ground slopes beyond it.

items.ask: How do you test stability of an equilibrium when d²Π/dq² = 0 at that point?
items.answer: The second-order test is inconclusive, so go to higher derivatives. The first nonzero derivative decides: even order and positive means stable; odd order means unstable. At a stable symmetric critical point d⁴Π/dq⁴ > 0.
items.cue: Flat-bottomed bowl: look further out. Even and positive curls up both sides; odd tips one side down.

items.ask: Give the small-θ post-buckling paths of the rigid bar with a base rotational spring and with a top lateral spring.
items.answer: Rotational spring: P/P_cr = θ/sin θ ≈ 1 + θ²/6, rising, stable symmetric, P_cr = C/L. Lateral spring: P/P_cr = cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2, falling, unstable symmetric, P_cr = kL.
items.cue: θ/sin θ grows from 1, cos θ shrinks from 1: rotational spring climbs, lateral spring sags.

items.ask: Sketch in words the load-deflection behaviour of the imperfect structure for each bifurcation type.
items.answer: Stable symmetric: deflection grows smoothly and the load rises past P_c. Unstable symmetric: a limit point below P_c, reduction ∝ ε^(2/3). Asymmetric: on the falling side a limit point below P_c, reduction ∝ ε^(1/2); on the other side a smooth rising path.
items.cue: Imperfect paths hug the perfect ones: they follow a rising branch up and peel off below a falling one.

items.ask: Define snap-through and give an example.
items.answer: Under load control at a limit point, the structure jumps dynamically to a distant stable equilibrium on another part of the path. Examples: shallow arch, two-bar (von Mises) truss, inflating balloon. Displacement control traces the descending branch.
items.cue: Press a jar lid or a shallow dome: it pops through all at once.

items.ask: A load is applied suddenly (as a step, held constant) to an undamped linear elastic system. What is the peak displacement?
items.answer: Twice the static displacement, δ_max = 2P/k. Energy balance: Pδ = ½kδ² at the turning point. The dynamic amplification factor is 2.
items.cue: Drop a weight onto a spring from contact: it overshoots to double, then oscillates about the static point.

items.ask: List the steps of the force (flexibility) method.
items.answer: 1) Count the degree of indeterminacy. 2) Release redundants to get a stable determinate primary structure. 3) Find release displacements δᵢ₀ under the real loads. 4) Find flexibilities fᵢⱼ from unit redundants. 5) Compatibility: δᵢ₀ + Σfᵢⱼ Xⱼ = 0. 6) Solve, then superpose.
items.cue: Cut, see the gap, find how hard each redundant closes it, then close it.

items.ask: List the steps of the displacement (stiffness) method.
items.answer: 1) Choose nodal displacement unknowns. 2) Form each element stiffness. 3) Assemble the global K. 4) Apply the displacement boundary conditions. 5) Solve Ku = f. 6) Recover member forces from element displacements.
items.cue: Unknown motions first, forces follow: the method a finite element code runs.

items.ask: How do you tell whether two elastic elements act in series or in parallel?
items.answer: Parallel: both undergo the same displacement and their forces add, so stiffnesses add. Series: both carry the same force and their displacements add, so compliances add.
items.cue: Same motion means side by side; same force means end to end, like links of a chain.

items.ask: How does a spring support of stiffness k behave in its two limits, and what does a flexible clamp need?
items.answer: Support displacement u = R/k. As k → ∞ it becomes a rigid support; as k → 0 the end becomes free. A flexible clamp is modelled by both a translational spring and a rotational spring.
items.cue: Turn the stiffness dial from zero to infinity and the end slides from free to fixed.

items.ask: How do you treat a rope or cable in an indeterminate structure?
items.answer: It carries tension only. Assume it taut, solve, and check the force is tensile. A compressive result means the rope is slack: re-solve with the rope removed.
items.cue: You can pull a rope; push it and it folds. Check the sign before trusting the answer.

items.ask: Fixed-fixed beam with a central point load P: give the end moment, midspan moment and midspan deflection.
items.answer: End moments PL/8 (hogging), midspan moment PL/8 (sagging), midspan deflection PL³/(192EI), one quarter of the simply supported value PL³/(48EI).
items.cue: Fixing the ends splits PL/4 evenly: half at the ends, half at the middle. 192 = 4 × 48.

items.ask: Give the stiffness of a close-coiled helical spring under axial load and under an end moment, and the wire loading in each.
items.answer: Axial: wire in torsion, k = Gd⁴/(8D³n). Moment (torsion spring): wire in bending, k_θ = Ed⁴/(64Dn) per radian. d wire diameter, D mean coil diameter, n active coils; wire length πDn.
items.cue: Pull a coil and the wire twists (G); twist a coil and the wire bends (E). Swap the loads, swap the modulus.

items.ask: In a curved beam under bending, where does the neutral axis move and where is the stress largest?
items.answer: The neutral axis shifts from the centroid toward the center of curvature. The stress distribution is hyperbolic and peaks at the inner fiber.
items.cue: Inner fibers are shorter, so the same rotation strains them more.

items.ask: When is the straight-beam flexure formula adequate for a curved beam?
items.answer: When the radius of curvature is large compared with the depth, R/h above about 10; the flexure formula is then within a few percent. For sharper curvature (hooks, links) use the Winkler formula.
items.cue: Ten depths of radius and the beam barely knows it is curved.

items.ask: How do you analyze a closed thin ring with Castigliano and least work?
items.answer: 1) Cut at a section of symmetry. 2) Symmetry fixes the shear there; statics fixes the normal force; the moment M₀ is the redundant. 3) Write M(θ) and U = ∫M²R dθ/(2EI). 4) Set ∂U/∂M₀ = 0. 5) Differentiate U by P for deflections.
items.cue: A closed ring is one big redundant loop: symmetry cuts it, least work closes it.

items.ask: Thin ring of radius R under equal and opposite diametral loads P: give the moments and the diametral change along the load.
items.answer: |M| = PR/π at the load points, |M| = PR(1/2 − 1/π) ≈ 0.18PR at 90° from them, of opposite sign. Change of diameter along P: (π/4 − 2/π)PR³/(EI) ≈ 0.149PR³/(EI).
items.cue: π shows up from integrating around the ring: 1/π ≈ 0.32 at the loads, the remainder of one half at the sides.

items.ask: List the steps of the transformed section method for a two-material beam.
items.answer: 1) Pick the reference material 1. 2) Scale material 2 widths by n = E₂/E₁, depths unchanged. 3) Find the centroid and I of the transformed section. 4) σ = My/I in the reference material. 5) Multiply by n for stress in material 2.
items.cue: Widen, solve as one material, then convert the stress back.

items.ask: Describe strain and stress across a bonded two-material beam in bending.
items.answer: Strain stays linear and continuous through the depth (perfect bond, plane sections). Stress = E × strain, so it jumps at the interface, higher in the stiffer material. The neutral axis moves toward the stiffer material.
items.cue: Strain is the shared ruler; stress is the ruler times each material's stiffness.

items.ask: Contrast a rigid joint and a pinned joint in a frame.
items.answer: A rigid joint transmits force and moment and keeps the angle between members fixed, so the members rotate together. A pinned joint transmits force only, carries zero moment and lets the members rotate relative to each other.
items.cue: Welded corner keeps its right angle; a hinge swings freely.

items.ask: List the assumptions of Euler column buckling.
items.answer: Perfectly straight prismatic column; axial load through the centroid; linear elastic material below the proportional limit; small deflections (curvature ≈ w″); conservative dead load; ideal end conditions.
items.cue: Straight, centred, elastic, small, dead load, ideal ends: a perfect column in a perfect world.

items.ask: Give the effective length factor K for the four classic end conditions.
items.answer: Pinned-pinned K = 1. Fixed-free (cantilever) K = 2. Fixed-pinned K ≈ 0.7 (0.699). Fixed-fixed K = 0.5.
items.cue: K is the gap between inflection points over L: a cantilever is half a pinned column of length 2L; fixed-fixed squeezes the sine to the middle half.

items.ask: Give the characteristic equation and critical load of a fixed-pinned column.
items.answer: tan kL = kL, smallest root kL = 4.493, so P_cr = 20.19EI/L² = 2.046π²EI/L², matching K = π/4.493 ≈ 0.7.
items.cue: 4.493 is where the tangent curve meets the 45° line on its second branch; squared, about 20.

items.ask: Give the buckling modes and loads of a pinned-pinned column.
items.answer: w = A sin(nπx/L), P_n = n²π²EI/L², n = 1, 2, 3, …. The first mode governs; a lateral brace at midspan forces mode 2 and quadruples P_cr.
items.cue: Guitar string harmonics: n half sine waves, load scales as n².

items.ask: List the steps to find a column's critical load from the differential equation.
items.answer: 1) Write EIw⁗ + Pw″ = 0, k² = P/(EI). 2) General solution w = A sin kx + B cos kx + Cx + D. 3) Apply four boundary conditions. 4) Homogeneous system: set the determinant to zero. 5) Smallest root gives P_cr; its eigenvector gives the mode.
items.cue: Four constants, four BCs, a zero determinant for a nonzero shape.

items.ask: Define the slenderness ratio and state about which axis a column buckles.
items.answer: Slenderness KL/r, with r = √(I/A) the radius of gyration. The column buckles about the axis with the largest KL/r, which for equal K and L is the axis of smallest I.
items.cue: A ruler under compression bows the floppy way, about its weak axis.

items.ask: Give the transition slenderness between the Johnson and Euler curves and the stress there.
items.answer: (KL/r)_t = √(2π²E/σ_y). There σ_cr = σ_y/2 and the Johnson parabola is tangent to the Euler hyperbola. Use Euler above it, Johnson below.
items.cue: Set π²E/s² equal to σ_y/2 and solve: s² = 2π²E/σ_y.

items.ask: Contrast the tangent modulus load, the reduced modulus load and Shanley's result for inelastic buckling.
items.answer: Tangent modulus: P_t = π²E_tI/(KL)², using the local slope E_t. Reduced modulus: P_r, using E_r between E_t and E, with P_t < P_r. Shanley: buckling begins at P_t, and the load rises toward P_r as bending grows; design uses P_t.
items.cue: Tangent is the doorway where bending starts; reduced is the ceiling the load climbs toward.

items.ask: Describe the load-deflection curves of pinned columns with different initial imperfections δ₀.
items.answer: Deflection grows from the start, w_max = δ₀/(1 − P/P_cr). Larger δ₀ gives larger deflection at every load. All curves approach P = P_cr asymptotically; the perfect column follows the bifurcation path.
items.cue: Every curve bends toward the same horizontal ceiling P_cr; a bigger initial bow just starts bending sooner.
